chunks: And with this chain, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Musa ibn Sa'dan, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, from Umar ibn Aban al-Kalbi, from Aban ibn Taghlib, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Surely, four thousand angels are at the grave of Husayn (peace be upon him), with disheveled hair and covered in dust, weeping until the Day of Judgment. Among them is an angel called Mansur. No visitor comes to visit him but they welcome him, and no one bids farewell but they escort him. No one falls ill but they visit him, and no one dies but they pray over his funeral and seek forgiveness for him after his death.'

key_terms.شُعْثٍ غُبْرٍ: Disheveled hair and covered in dust, indicating a state of mourning or distress
key_terms.مَنْصُورٌ: Mansur (the name of the leading angel)
key_terms.يَزُورُهُ زَائِرٌ: A visitor visits him (referring to Ziyarat)

ai.seo_question: What is the role of the angels at the grave of Imam Husayn (a.s.) according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq highlights the perpetual cosmic mourning at Karbala, where four thousand angels, led by Mansur, serve as eternal attendants to Imam Husayn (a.s.). Their continuous actions—welcoming visitors, escorting the departing, and praying for the deceased—underscore the spiritual vitality of the shrine and the interconnectedness of the living and the dead in Shia devotional practice.
